proxy_language: Unidentified: 'Saertulmach' is not an attested language or culture name in Glottolog, ASJP or any standard Americanist source. Fallback proxy is the Mapudungun (Mapuche, Araucanian) language of south-central Chile and Argentina, in the Araucanian family, in its colonial-to-modern attested form.
proxy_rationale: The label gives no ethnolinguistic anchor. The region is 'The Americas' and the kind is 'later_court' at period index 6, i.e. a late, politically organised, court-like society. Aztec/Nahuatl, Quechua, Maya and Mapudungun are all defensible 'later' American proxies; Mapudungun is chosen because it has a well-described grammar (Smeets 2008, Zuniga 2006) and a documented lexicon (Augusta 1916, Febres 1765), and its phonology and agglutinative morphology allow principled name-building. The existing game names (Jollof rice, Egusi soup, Fufu, Suya, Waakye, Akara) are West African dishes and are linguistically irrelevant here; they must be discarded, not mimicked. This link is purely a modelling convenience, not a claim that the Saertulmach spoke Mapudungun.
phonology: Consonants (Zuniga 2006 / Smeets 2008 style): stops p t ch (palatal affricate) k, plus retroflex-ish tr (affricate) and interdental-ish dental t; fricatives f, th (interdental), s, sh (rare), v (voiced, often glide-like); nasals m n nh ng (velar, written ng) ; lateral l, ll (interdental-lateral variant); rhotic r (retroflex approximant, written r); glides w y. Vowels: a e i o u and the high central unrounded vowel written ü; no phonemic length or tone. Stress is on the second syllable of a word in the usual analysis and does not affect spelling.
phonotactics: Syllable shapes: (C)V(C), i.e. V, CV, VC, CVC. Onsets are single consonants; no tautosyllabic clusters. Codas are single consonants (typically n, l, m, ng, k, f, s, r) and medial heterosyllabic clusters such as -nk-, -lk-, -mp- occur across syllable boundaries. Words may end in a vowel or a consonant (n, l, m, ng, k, f, r, s all occur). Native lexemes are mostly bisyllabic roots; verbs carry long suffix chains, nouns are short.
orthography: Use a simplified Azumchefe-style practical orthography for Mapudungun in Latin script: a e i o u ü; p t k ch tr f s th l ll m n ng ñ r w y v. Digraphs ch, tr, th, ll, ng, ñ are single units. No c, b, d, g (except inside ng), h, j, q, x, z, and no doubled vowels as length marks.
morphology: Agglutinative and mostly suffixing. Nouns are uninflected for case; number is optional (-pu plural marker, or the enumerating word pu in front of the noun) and possession is marked by pronoun order. Verbs bear derivational and inflectional suffixes (-n infinitive/1sg indicative nominaliser, -we instrumental/locative nominaliser, -fe agent, -el patient/relative, -m for causative -m, -tu repetitive/transitive, -nge copular/passive). Reduplication is rare and mostly expressive. There are no noun classes or grammatical gender.
compounding: Noun-noun compounds are head-final: modifier + head (mapu 'land' + che 'people' = mapuche 'people of the land'). Agentive 'X-er' names use root + -fe (kellu-fe 'helper'; ngillatu-fe 'one who prays'). Instrument/place names use verb root + -we (ngillatu-we 'place of praying', rüpü-we 'path'). 'X of Y' is expressed by direct juxtaposition Y X (possessor before possessed, no linker): antü ruka 'sun house'. Adjectives follow nouns only in lexicalised pairs; productive modification is by juxtaposition with the modifier first. Name-compounds join with a hyphen or are written solid.
noun_phrase_order: Possessor/modifier + head noun (modifier-first, head-final), e.g. ngen 'owner' follows the owned: mapu ngen 'owner of the land'. Numerals precede the noun (kula 'three' + ruka 'house'). The plural marker pu precedes the noun. Demonstratives precede the noun.

Augusta, Fray Felix Jose de. Diccionario Araucano-Espanol y Espanol-Araucano. Santiago, 1916
Febres, Andres. Arte de la lengua general del Reyno de Chile. Lima, 1765
notes: Saertulmach is not an attested culture; all constraints are a modelling convenience based on Mapudungun and must not be presented as a real language of that culture. No Goidelic restriction applies, but no generated word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word. The existing West African dish names (Jollof rice, Egusi soup, Fufu, Suya, Waakye, Akara) are unrelated and should be replaced.
